![](featured.png)

[imbalanced-learn-extra](https://github.com/georgedouzas/imbalanced-learn-extra) extends
[imbalanced-learn](https://imbalanced-learn.org/stable/) with oversamplers it leaves out, usually because they are newer or less
cited. It has two main parts.

The first is a general interface for clustering-based oversampling. [SMOTE](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1106.1813.pdf) and its variants
only look at the imbalance between classes, but a class can also be imbalanced within itself. Clustering the data first helps with
that. You can combine any clusterer with any oversampler, so here is k-means with SMOTE:

```python
from collections import Counter
from imblearn.over_sampling import SMOTE
from imblearn_extra.clover.over_sampling import ClusterOverSampler
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer

X, y = load_breast_cancer(return_X_y=True)
print(Counter(y.tolist()))

oversampler = ClusterOverSampler(
    oversampler=SMOTE(random_state=0), clusterer=KMeans(n_clusters=10, random_state=0, n_init=10)
)
_, y_resampled = oversampler.fit_resample(X, y)
print(Counter(y_resampled.tolist()))
```

```
Counter({1: 357, 0: 212})
Counter({0: 357, 1: 357})
```

The second is [Geometric SMOTE](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ins.2019.06.007). SMOTE creates new samples
by interpolating on a line between existing ones. Geometric SMOTE expands that area, and it works as a drop-in replacement:

```python
from collections import Counter
from imblearn_extra.gsmote import GeometricSMOTE
from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer

X, y = load_breast_cancer(return_X_y=True)
_, y_resampled = GeometricSMOTE(random_state=0).fit_resample(X, y)
print(Counter(y_resampled.tolist()))
```

```
Counter({0: 357, 1: 357})
```

Both follow the imbalanced-learn API, so they fit into scikit-learn style pipelines. Install it with
`pip install imbalanced-learn-extra`.
